AfriScan · Zambia · Wayleaves, reserves and licence areas

Know what is being built inside your wayleaves and rights of way in Zambia

AfriScan maps structures, excavations, cleared ground and new tracks along power lines, pipelines, railways and roads, and across mining licence areas in Zambia. Each structure gets coordinates and its distance to your line or boundary, each stretch of the route gets an encroachment-density rating, and dated surveys show what is new. A person reviews every result before you receive a PDF report and GIS files your wayleave, land and community-relations teams can use.

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work Electricity (Wayleave and Clearances) Regulations 2026 · ERB siting guidelines for petroleum pipelines · Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024 · Tanzania-Zambia Railway Act · ZCARs Part 18 · Data Protection Act 2021 · IFC Performance Standard 5

The widths are in the law

What Zambian law says about building in wayleaves, rights of way and reserves

Zambia’s rules set widths, distances and consents that a dated structure register can be measured against. These are the four that come up most.

SI No. 2 of 2026

Power-line wayleaves have minimum widths

The Electricity (Wayleave and Clearances) Regulations 2026 set minimum wayleave widths by voltage, for example 32 m for a 132 kV line, 48 m for 330 kV and 50 m for 400 kV, and wider strips where a line crosses a recognised forestry area. Under the Electricity Act 2019, no one may put up a building or structure that is likely to interfere with a line without the licensee’s permission (s.26).

ERB siting guidelines

New pipeline routes avoid settlements

The Energy Regulation Board’s Guidelines for Siting Petroleum Infrastructure say a new petroleum pipeline route shall be such that the pipeline “does not pass through settlements”, and must leave enough land for a right of way under Zambian Standard ZS 704 (s.5.7).

MRC Act 2024, s.35

Mining needs consent near homes and railways

Under the Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024, a mining-right holder needs written consent before working within 180 m of an occupied house, within 100 m of a railway track, or on village and customary land.

TAZARA Act, s.62

The railway strip is kept clear

Under the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Act, no building, structure or works may be put on the railway strip without the Authority’s written permission.

Each of those rules turns on the same facts: what stands on the ground, where, how close to the line or boundary, and since when. That is what a dated register records. For the widths and consents in detail, read our guide to wayleaves, reserves and rights of way in Zambia.

What you get

A dated register your wayleave, land and GIS teams can use

  • A wayleave or right-of-way register: each structure with an ID, its distance to the line, its band, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and UTM.
  • A rating for every 500 m of the route, high, medium or low for encroachment density, so your teams know which stretches to visit first. It is a count rule, not a safety rating.
  • Licence-area surveys: structures inside your mining licence area or site and in a ring around it.
  • Route options compared by the structures each alignment would affect, before the route is fixed.
  • Change between dated surveys: new and removed structures, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.
  • Excavation mapping: pits, spoil heaps and disturbed ground, with new sites flagged between dates.
  • A cut-off-date baseline for resettlement, with the imagery date on every record.
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers, plus an interactive map file that opens in a browser.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, excavations, cleared ground, tracks and vegetation change. We do not identify, count or follow people, and satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or who did anything. Whether a structure is authorised is for you, the licensee, the authorities and, if it comes to that, the courts. Our registers support your wayleave, compensation, legal and community processes; they do not replace any of them.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds before anything is delivered. What imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled re-surveys

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one saying what changed.

Protected sites respected

On declared protected places and areas we work only for, or with the written authority of, the operator, and security sites are masked in every deliverable.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Send the route or boundary

    The line, pipeline or reserve route, or the licence-area boundary, with the widths and the date the record must reflect. We agree the bands, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Satellite screening

    Structures, excavations and cleared ground are mapped along the whole route from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold.

  3. Drone detail where needed

    Stretches that need more detail than satellite imagery shows are flown, subject to the ZCAA approvals and Zambia Air Force clearance each operation requires.

  4. A person reviews every result

    A reviewer confirms, corrects and adds to every automatic result, and each structure is measured, banded and rated. The PDF report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name, and re-surveys follow the schedule you set.

In the rainy season, cloud can delay optical imagery; radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up once clearer imagery is available. More on how it works, the methodology and imagery and data sources.

Drones in Zambia

Satellite first, drones under ZCARs Part 18

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. No aircraft flies, so no special authorisation or Air Force clearance is needed, however long the wayleave.

Drone detail. Drone surveys in Zambia need ZCAA approvals for the operator, every aircraft and every pilot: an RPAS Operator Certificate with its operations specifications, an Air Services Permit for commercial work, a registration and Letter of Approval for each drone, and a Remote Pilot Licence for each pilot. Each operation also needs a ZCAA special authorisation, a ZCAA inspector on site and Zambia Air Force airspace clearance. Flights within 50 m of structures, people or public roads need specific approval or permission, which matters along any wayleave lined with homes.

Afridrone is working towards the ZCAA approvals Zambia requires. Every drone proposal names the Zambian company that will fly it and its approvals, so your team can check them.

The Zambian drone-law guide

The six approvals, the 2026 circulars, the 50 m rules, protected places and an 11-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, as of 27 September 2026.

Drone law in Zambia

For procurement and compliance teams

Tenders, local content and data

Public tenders in Zambia limit open national bidding to citizen and local bidders, mining companies must reserve a growing share of their procurement for local companies under SI 68 of 2025, and the Data Protection Act 2021 requires personal data to be processed and stored in Zambia, with exceptions the Minister may prescribe. Our notes set out what applies to this kind of service, where the main public buyers advertise, and what to ask any supplier for.

Working with AfriScan in Zambia

We respond to requests for proposals and tenders. Send your supplier or prequalification forms with your request; the proposal states the contracting structure for your tender and which registrations are in place for your contract.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Zambia?

The ones that apply to your asset. For power lines we default to the minimum wayleave for the voltage in the Electricity (Wayleave and Clearances) Regulations 2026, such as 32 m for 132 kV, 48 m for 330 kV and 50 m for 400 kV, or the wider strip in a recognised forestry area. For pipelines, railways and roads we measure from the centreline or reserve boundary you supply, at your easement or reserve widths, and for licence areas from the boundary. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey, each structure with its distance and band.

Does a satellite survey need ZCAA approval?

No aircraft is flown, so the drone rules in Part 18 of the Zambia Civil Aviation Requirements do not apply to the satellite work itself, and satellite-based wayleave and right-of-way screening is available across Zambia (Zambian counsel should confirm this for any corridor or site declared a protected place or area). Drone stretches, where you want them, are planned separately and are subject to the ZCAA approvals and Zambia Air Force clearance each operation requires.

Can you tell us which structures are unauthorised?

No. We map what stands where, how far it is from your line or boundary, and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether it has the licensee’s permission under the Electricity Act, the railway authority’s written permission or the licence holder’s consent, or predates the wayleave, is for your land and legal teams and the authorities to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

Our corridor is a declared protected area. Can you still work on it?

Some pipeline corridors, pumping stations, mine workings and bridges in Zambia are covered by orders printed in the consolidated Protected Places and Areas Act; whether each is still in force is for Zambian counsel. We work there only for, or with the written authority of, the operator or licence holder, and security sites are masked in every deliverable.

Do you detect vandalism or theft on lines and pipelines?

No. Satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or people. We map land change, such as new structures, fresh excavations, cleared ground and new tracks, so your patrols know where to look first.

How is personal data handled under the Data Protection Act?

Our registers describe structures, not people, and carry no names. Imagery of homes linked to names, census lists or grievance files is personal data under the Data Protection Act 2021, which requires registration and storage in Zambia unless an exception applies; whether any other layer is personal data for your project is for your data protection officer or counsel. Each proposal sets out the controller and processor roles, where project data will be stored and how results are shared. See working with AfriScan in Zambia.

Is the register a land survey?

No. The Land Survey Act requires the Surveyor-General’s written permission before aerial photography is used for land survey, and our registers are not land surveys or cadastral plans. They are monitoring and planning records built from imagery, which show your surveyors and wayleave officers where to look.

Know what stands in your wayleave while it is still one structure.

Send the line, pipeline or reserve route, or the licence-area boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the province and district, and the widths that apply: the SI 2 of 2026 wayleave for the voltage, your easement or reserve widths, or a distance your engineers set. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
